record.stem: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse
record.central_claim: The simultaneous all-time highs across multiple asset classes and goods are not the result of multiple independent bubbles, but rather a consequence of the declining purchasing power of the U.S. dollar.

themes.theme: Pervasive price increases across assets and goods

arguments.conclusion: The synchronous all-time highs in diverse assets and goods indicate a common cause rather than multiple independent bubbles.

US Case Shiller home price index at all-time highs; median sale price of houses near 2022 high.
Cost of rent, ground beef, electricity, college tuition, and health insurance are all at all-time highs.

analogies.explanation: Compares the broad-based nature of current price increases to past narrow bubbles (dot-com, crypto 2017) to illustrate that this pattern is different and suggests a systemic cause.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: Historically, when there is a bubble, it is an outlier. When you looked at the dot bubble and within the course of just a few years, the value of the NASDAQ went from 1,000 all the way up to almost 5,000. You could tell that that was crazy because other assets not exposed to that sector, like if you looked at the Dow Jones Industrial Average, did not have the exact same thing occur. ... Similarly, when the big crypto bubble happened in 2017 and Bitcoin went from just a couple of thousand all the way up to almost 20,000 within the course of about a year, you were able to tell that it was a bubble because it wasn't happening everywhere.

arguments.conclusion: The dollar's declining purchasing power, rather than asset overvaluation, explains the widespread price increases.
premises: When everything is expensive relative to the dollar, the comparison point is the dollar.
The DXY (dollar index) has been stable because other currencies are also devalued, masking the dollar's loss of value.
Pricing assets in gold reveals that many are not at bubble levels.

evidence.item: DXY chart shows the dollar at the same level as 2015.
evidence.verification_basis: Transcript describes the pattern and explains its interpretation.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Now, you might be thinking, well, if you pull up a chart of the dollar, it really hasn't done much. In fact, it's at the exact same level it was back in 2015. It's had a little bit of volatility, but it's not falling through the floor like you might expect given the price of everything.

evidence.item: Comparison of DXY to other fiat currencies explains why it doesn't show dollar weakness.
evidence.verification_basis: Transcript provides reasoning based on relative currency devaluation.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: The reason for this is because again, you have to ask the question compared to what? When you look at this chart of the dollar, you are comparing the dollar to other currencies around the world. That's what the DXY is, the dollar index. it's a dollar versus a basket of other fiat currencies. Which means this chart looks pretty much exactly like what you should expect because if every government and central bank around the world is devaluing their own currency at around approximately the same rate, of course you're not going to have that large of fluctuations in the value of one currency compared to another, which is why the DXY doesn't look anything crazy.

analogies.explanation: The dollar is described as a 'measuring stick' or 'denominator' that has changed length, making everything else seem inflated.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: Maybe the real problem is in your measuring stick. Maybe the real problem lies with your denominator, your currency, the dollar.

analogies.explanation: Used repeatedly to direct attention to the dollar as the common reference point for all price comparisons.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: The point is the question that you should always be asking yourself when you are trying to figure out if something is expensive is compared to what?

arguments.conclusion: The current buying behavior across assets and goods matches von Mises' description of a 'flight into real goods' or crack-up boom, driven by expectations of continued dollar depreciation.
premises: Von Mises stated that once the public is convinced money supply increases will continue, everyone tries to buy as much as possible to avoid holding cash.
People with means buy assets; those without means deal with higher cost of living.
This is the phenomenon seen in America today, though not hyperinflation.

evidence.item: Direct quote of Ludwig von Mises describing the crack-up boom.
evidence.verification_basis: Exact quote provided in transcript.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: He said if once public opinion is convinced that the increase in the quantity of money will continue and never come to an end and that consequently the prices of all commodities and services will not cease to rise. Everybody becomes eager to buy as much as possible and to restrict his cash holding to a minimum size. For under these circumstances, the regular costs incurred by holding cash are increased by the losses caused by the progressive fall in purchasing power. The advantages of holding cash must be paid for by sacrifices which are deemed unreasonably burdensome. This phenomenon was in the great European inflations of the 20s called flight into real goods or crackup boom.

evidence.item: Description of current American behavior: rich buy assets, poor bear higher costs.
evidence.verification_basis: Transcript states this as observation; no external source but internally coherent.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Those who have the means to do so are buying assets to protect their money and those who do not have the means to do so are dealing with the consequences of that inflation by buying goods. In other words, cost of living at the higher and higher prices.

analogies.device: Historical analogy to European inflations of the 1920s
analogies.explanation: Compares current US situation to the 'flight into real goods' seen in great European inflations, as described by von Mises.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: This phenomenon was in the great European inflations of the 20s called flight into real goods or crackup boom. ... While we are not experiencing anything closely related to what could be called hyperinflation, this is the phenomenon that we are seeing happen in America today.

arguments.conclusion: Given M2 money supply growth returning to the normal 5-10% range and expected Fed rate cuts, the decline in dollar purchasing power is likely to continue, making a deflationary crash unlikely.
premises: M2 money supply has reached a new all-time high after a brief decline in 2023.
The year-over-year growth rate bottomed at -4.87% in 2023 and is now back to 5-10%.
The Federal Reserve is expected to cut rates, which encourages borrowing and money creation.
A deflationary scenario would require the government to stop borrowing and spending, which is politically and economically unlikely.

evidence.item: M2 money supply now at a new all-time high, surpassing the 2022 high.
evidence.verification_basis: Transcript references Federal Reserve chart; no specific numeric value given but trend is described.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: This is simply a chart put out by the Federal Reserve that shows the total supply of US dollars in the US financial system. ... the money supply is now at a new all-time high, eclipsing the high that it hit in 2022.

evidence.item: Growth rate of US money supply peaked at 27% in 2021, bottomed at -4.87% in 2023, now back to 5-10%.
evidence.verification_basis: Exact percentages provided in the transcript.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: the growth rate of the US money supply is between 5 to 10% per year. It peaked in 2021 at 27% year-over-year growth. And it bottomed in 2023 at a decline of 4.87%

evidence.item: Expectation that Fed will cut rates, fueling money supply growth.
evidence.verification_basis: Market expectation referenced but no source or explicit basis provided in transcript.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: especially considering that the Federal Reserve is largely expected to begin cutting rates very soon.

evidence.item: Scenario that a deflationary crash would rival the Great Depression and is unlikely.
evidence.verification_basis: Speculative statement about future policy decisions and economic outcomes; no evidence provided.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20250912_It’s Not an Everything Bubble, it’s a Dollar Collapse.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: you would need to expect that policymakers would be okay with and would allow a deflationary death spiral that would rival or perhaps exceed the Great Depression to just happen again. And while I guess that's technically possible, I don't think that it's anywhere near the most likely outcome, which means I don't think we are in the midst of a bubble getting ready to pop.
